Early Results Of a Phase I/II Trial Of Midostaurin (PKC412) and 5-Azacytidine (5-AZA)For Patients (Pts) With Acute Myeloid Leukemia and Myelodysplastic Syndrome.↵55th Annual Meeting of the American Society of Hematology (ASH).↵The investigators reported the results of a phase I/II trial of Midostaurin (PKC412) and 5-Azacytidine (5-AZA) for patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS).↵Background: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) and  affects primarily elderly patient's.↵Their treatment with aggressive chemotherapy was frequently challenging.↵Moreover, patient's with FLT3 mutations had very poor prognosis.↵The authors hypothesized that the combination of midostaurin, a FLT3 inhibitor, and 5-AZA, a hypomethylating agent, may be an effective and safe regimen.↵Methods: Both untreated (8) and previously treated (36) patient's with AML or MDS were eligible for this study, regardless of FLT3 mutation and prior exposure to FLT3 inhibitors.↵Patient's received 5-AZA 75 mg/mq subcutaneously or intravenously on day 1-7 and midostaurin 25 mg bid (in cohort 1 of phase I) or 50 mg bid (in cohort 2 of Phase I and in Phase II) orally on day 8-21 during the first cycle and continuously thereafter, for 12 cycles of 28 days duration.↵Cytogenetic risk was defined according to MRC criteria.↵Differences between categorical variables were compared by the chi2 test.↵CR duration (CRD) was calculated from the time of CR achievement until relapse and estimated by the Kaplan-Meier method and compared by the log-rank test.↵Results.↵Fourty-four patient's were enrolled, 13 included in Phase I and 31 in Phase II.↵Thirty-eight pts (86%) received 50 mg bid of midostaurin, and 6 (14%; Phase I) received 25 mg bid.↵The median number of administered cycles was 2.↵Grade 3-4 hematological toxicities consisted of 95% neutropenia, 64% anemia and 93% thrombocytopenia.↵Grade 3-4 non-hematological toxicities consisted of 45% infections, 23% hypokalemia, 16% hyponatremia, 7% reduction in ejection fraction, 7% hyperuricemia, 4% hyperglycemia, 4% nausea/vomiting, 4% QTc prolongation, 4% hyperbilirubinemia, and 4% elevated AST.↵Eleven patient's (25%) achieved a CR, 9 with incomplete platelet recovery (20%), after a median time of 13 weeks from treatment start.↵Five (11%) of these patient's relapsed after achieving CR.↵Two patient's (5%) received an allogeneic stem cell transplant while on study, one in CR and one primary refractory (after a blast count drop from 27 to 7%), and they are both still in CR and alive.↵Among 26 patient's with FLT3 ITD and no D835 mutation, 9 (35%) achieved CR/CRp.↵Six of 18 (33%) patient's not previously exposed to FLT3 inhibitors responded.↵There was no significant correlation of dose with response (24% with 50 mg bid versus 33% with 25 mg bid, p equals 0.63).↵After a median follow-up of 15 weeks, 20 patient's (64%) died, 3 (7%) while on study (2 died of sepsis, 1 of unknown causes with progressive disease).↵The median CRD was 16 months.↵Factors significantly associated with a longer CRD were male sex (p equals 0.04), age older than 65 years (0.03) and use of 50 mg bid of midostaurin (p equals 0.02).↵Conclusions.↵The combination of midostaurin and 5-AZA was safe and well tolerated.↵Its efficacy was most noticeable among patient's with FLT3 mutations.↵A longer response duration was observed using midostaurin at 50 mg bid dose and in elderly male patient's.↵The investigators did not provide an assessment of the causal relationship between the events and therapy.↵GAST↵

Historical condition included treatment with unspecified medication but presented with no improvement.

On an unknown date, patient experienced <AE>pain</AE> (see case: PHHY2016PA085952), <AE>weight decreased</AE> (see case: PHHY2016PA142518) and <AE>stomachache</AE> (see case: PHHY2016PA051512).
The patient received <TREATMENT>tramadol</TREATMENT> (manufacturer unknown) for the treatment of <IND>pain</IND> due to arm operation from an unknown start date at an unknown dose (route: unknown).
It was reported that, patient restarted the treatment with <SDRUG>Afinitor</SDRUG> as unknown dose, frequency and route on 13 Feb 2016.
On 29 Oct 2016, the patient broke an arm (<AE>hand fracture</AE>) as a consequence of a fall due to a misstep and was left facing up and even hurt his head (<AE>head injury</AE>) as it was a whip movement.
The patient was taken to the hospital and was admitted to have surgery performed.
The patient also had slightly decreased <LAB>hemoglobin level</LAB> (<AE>haemoglobin decreased</AE>) and for his surgery preparation he was indicated 1 IV iron ampoule iron for 3 weeks.
The patient’s <LAB>sugar values</LAB> are normal and his <LAB>hemoglobin</LAB> was increasing (unknown values).
On an unknown date, the patient had a <DX>CAT (computerised tomogram)</DX> performed (results pending) and today (24 Nov 2016) he was going to have some lab controls performed and would take them with him to an oncologist appointment.

On 15 Jan (year unspecified) the patient got so <AE>unwell</AE> that an ambulance had to be called, this happened 2 more times.
Upon follow up, it was reported that the <SDRUG>Afinitor</SDRUG> continued to be suspended until new evaluation.
It was mentioned that the <AE>pain</AE> after surgery diminished considerably.
Currently he was taking <TREATMENT>Panadol</TREATMENT> (<DOSE>1 oral tablet every 6 hours</DOSE>) and <TREATMENT>tramadol</TREATMENT> (<DOSE>1 oral tablet at night</DOSE>), without problems.

A 83 year old male patient experienced serious events of Hypoglycemia and Acute Onset Of Confusion while being treated with Levothyrox 25 (25 microgram). Seriousness criteria: Hypoglycemia (hospitalization) and Acute Onset Of Confusion (hospitalization). Medical history: Hypercholesterolaemia, Anxiodepressive Syndrome, Sleep Apnoea Syndromes, Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, Hypertension Arterial and AFib. Concomitant medications: Calcidose (colecalciferol, calcium carbonate), Prozac (fluoxetine hydrochloride) and Lovenox (enoxaparine sodique ((mammifere/porc/muqueuse intestinale)), enoxaparin sodium). 
Kindly refer to the concomitant medication section for therapy details.
The patient received Levothyrox 25 (levothyroxine sodium) 25 microgram, at one dosage form a day orally since an unknown date for hypothyroidism.
Additionally, the patient received the following non-Merck suspected drugs: Tramadol (tramadol) at an unknown dose orally since an unknown date for pain.
Imovane (zopiclone) 3.75 milligram, at one dosage form a day orally since 03 Oct 2017 for anxiodepressive syndrome.
Pantoprazole (pantoprazole) at a dosage of 40 milligram a day orally since 25 Sep 2017 for unknown indication.
Amarel (glimepiride) 1 milligram, at a dosage of one dosage form a day orally since an unknown date for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
Linezolide (linezolid) at a dosage of 1200 milligram a day orally since 20 Oct 2017 for osteitis.
Tygacil (tigecycline) 50 milligram, at a dosage of 200 milligram a day, Intravenous (not otherwise specified) since 25 Oct 2017 for osteitis.
Bisoprolol Hemifumarate (bisoprolol fumarate) at a dosage of 10 milligram a day orally since an unknown date for AFib. The patient experienced the following serious event: Hypoglycemia and Acute Onset Of Confusion Started on 30 Oct 2017.
On 30 Oct 2017, the patient experienced hypoglycemia and acute onset of confusion.
On 30 Oct 2017 the patient's hypoglycemia showed 0.69 g/L, on 01 Nov 2017, the patient underwent blood test and hypoglycemia showed 0.63 g/L, on 03 Nov 2017, the patient's hypoglycemia showed 0.62 g/L, on 07 Nov 2017, the patient's hypoglycemia showed 0.71 g/L. Action taken with Amarel in response to Hypoglycemia, Acute Onset Of Confusion: Drug discontinued on 03 Nov 2017. Action taken with Bisoprolol in response to Hypoglycemia, Acute Onset Of Confusion: Dose Reduced. Outcome of the events: Acute Onset Of Confusion: Resolved on Nov 2017. Hypoglycemia: Resolved on 07 Nov 2017. Reporter's causality assessment: Relationship with Levothyrox 25, Tramadol, Imovane, Pantoprazole, Amarel, Linezolide, Tygacil, and Bisoprolol for the events Hypoglycemia, Acute Onset Of Confusion: Not Reported. llm_output:
FR-NAPPMUNDI-GBR-2019-0066507 is a literature spontaneous report received in the form of a full article on 09MAY2019 in France.
This article refers to a <AGE>56-year-old</AGE> <SEX>female</SEX> patient, who experienced <AE>completed suicide</AE>, <AE>hypoglycaemia</AE> while using <SDRUG>morphine sulfate</SDRUG> and was reported as follows:
"A <AGE>56-year-old</AGE> nurse with suicidal tendencies was found dead in her car 24 hours after disappearing.
An empty bottle of whiskey, empty <ODRUG>alprazolam</ODRUG> blisters and <SDRUG>insulin</SDRUG> pens were found near the corpse.
Autopsy showed common signs of toxic death.
Three needle marks were found on the left arm, and were sampled along with the usual toxicological matrices.
Methods: General toxicological screening was performed to screen for ethanol, carbon monoxide, medical drugs and drugs of abuse.
<LAB>Glucose</LAB> and <LAB>lactate</LAB> in vitreous humor (VH) and <LAB>glycated hemoglobin (HBA1c)</LAB> in whole blood were quantified by an enzymatic method on a Cobas analyzer.
Immunoassay (Cobas) was performed on femoral blood (FB) serum to screen for <LAB>insulin</LAB> and <LAB>C-peptide</LAB>.
For <LAB>insulin</LAB> assay in injection site tissue, 1 g of tissue was pretreated by grinding and ultrasonic bath in an acid ethanol solution; then solid phase extraction by anion exchange was performed before analysis on LC/HRMS [liquid chromatography coupled to an exactive high-resolution/high accuracy mass spectrometry].
Result: Ethanol was detected only in urine, at 0.11 g/L.
Ethylglucuronide was quantified at 0.06 mcg/mL and 133 mcg/mL in FB and urine, respectively.
<ODRUG>Alprazolam</ODRUG> (45 ng/mL) and <CDRUG>tramadol</CDRUG> (270 ng/mL) were found in FB.
<MHX>Morphine</MHX> and <MHX>codeine</MHX> were quantified in urine at 102 ng/mL and 290 ng/mL respectively, but not detected in FB.
<LAB>HBA1c level</LAB> was 4.5%.
<LAB>Glucose assay</LAB> was negative (< 0.10 mmol/L) in both VH samples.
<LAB>Lactate</LAB> was quantified at 10.3 and 9.9 mmol/L in right and left VH, respectively.
<LAB>Serum immunoassays</LAB> were negative for <LAB>insulin</LAB> (< 1 mU/L) and <LAB>C-peptide</LAB> (< 0.03 nmol/L).
Analysis of suspected injection site tissue identified <SDRUG>aspart</SDRUG>, an <SDRUG>insulin</SDRUG> analog.
Discussion: <ODRUG>Alprazolam</ODRUG> and <CDRUG>tramadol</CDRUG> concentrations were subtoxic in blood; opiates and ethanol were detected only in urine.
Toxic death was not demonstrated from these Results.
The values of <LAB>glucose</LAB> and <LAB>lactate</LAB> in vitreous humor suggested a potentially lethal <AE>hypoglycemic state</AE>, according to the reference values [...].
However, despite the <SDRUG>insulin</SDRUG> pens found in the car, <LAB>insulin immunoassay</LAB> was negative in blood.
Injection site analysis by LC/HRMS allowed identification of the <SDRUG>insulin</SDRUG> analog, <SDRUG>aspart</SDRUG>.
This finding of <SDRUG>insulin</SDRUG> analog intake in a non-diabetic subject, associated with the <LAB>glucose</LAB> and <LAB>lactate</LAB> concentrations in VH, suggested severe <mAE>hypoglycemia</mAE> induced by <SDRUG>insulin</SDRUG> analog injection.
Various hypotheses could explain the failure to detect <SDRUG>aspart</SDRUG> in serum: the poor ability of immunoassay to detect analogs metabolism during the time between injection and death, and/or degradation by hemolysis during the postmortem interval.
Conclusion: [...] In the present case, the medicolegal examiner diagnosed a <AE>hypoglycemic state</AE> with fatal outcome secondary to <SDRUG>aspart</SDRUG> injection as <COD>cause of death</COD>, and <AE>suicide</AE> as the manner."
The reporter considered <AE>hypoglycaemia</AE> to be not reasonably related to <SDRUG>morphine sulfate</SDRUG> use.
The reporter did not provide a causality assessment between <AE>completed suicide</AE> and <SDRUG>morphine sulfate</SDRUG> use.
Mundipharma Research considered the causality between the <AE>adverse events</AE> and <SDRUG>morphine sulfate</SDRUG> use as not assessable.
The case was rated to be serious as <AE>completed suicide</AE>, <AE>hypoglycaemia</AE> resulted in death; <AE>completed suicide</AE>, <AE>hypoglycaemia</AE> were considered to be medically significant.
Additional information has been requested.
This case will be updated accordingly should more information become available.
Citation: DOI: 10.1016/j.toxac.2019.03.043 Bottinelli C, Guitton J, Fanton L, Bevalot F; Characterization of suicide involving insulin analog injection: Interest of injection site analysis by LC/HRMS; Toxicologie Analytique et Clinique; 2019; 31(2):34-35.

On admission in the emergency ward, ASAT was at 14N, ALAT at 11N, alkaline phosphatasis was normal, total bilirubin was at 3N, hypoglycaemia at 1.1mmol/l, hypokalemia at 2.7mmol/l, PT at 47%, paracetamolemia at 04h49pm was at 62mg/l.
She was transferred into another hospital in the hepatologic intensive unit.
Glasgow was at 15, serum ethanol was lower than 0.1g/l at 08:30pm, paracetamolemia was 46mcg/ml, PT was 30% and Factor V was at 15%.
On 08-Feb-2010, the EEG did not evidence any <R/O>encephalopathy</R/O>.
Brain scan was unremarkable.
On 09-Feb-2010 her situation worsened with PT lower than 10%, Factor V lower than 5%, ASAT at 308 N, ALAT at 190 N and total bilirubin at 5.8 N.
She evolved clinically with state II encephalopathy.
This same day, 09-Feb-2010, she was enrolled in a hepatic graft wait list.
On 10-Feb-2010 her situation worsened even more, she was intubated and received neurological protection measures.
On 11-Feb-2010 she received a hepatic graft.
Anatomopathological analysis of hepatectomised liver showed submassive hepatocytes necrosis lesions with histological aspect similar to the one usually described on paracetamol overdose.
She was discharged on 06-Mar-2010, recovered with sequelae.
Keppra and tramadol/paracetamol were stopped.
The events were considered as life threatening.
The Afssaps considered the events as dubiously related to Keppra and Ixprim.

Posters / Leukemia Research 35 (2011) S27-S142.↵The authors report the results of a phase I, open label, multicenter, dose escalation study assessing the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and safety of PAN in combination with 5-aza in patients with MDS, chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML), and AML.↵Inclusion criteria of this ongoing study were: adult patients with IPSS intermediate-2 or high-risk MDS, CMML, or AML with 20-30% marrow blasts not eligible for hematopoetic stem-cell transplantation.↵Oral PAN (20 mg/day starting dose) was administered during a 28-day cycle on Days 3, 5, 8, 10, 12, and 15 in combination with a fixed dose of 5-aza (75mg/m2 SC) on days 1-7 of each cycle.↵Safety and tolerability are described as type, duration, frequency, relatedness, and severity of adverse events (AEs) according to CTCAE, v3.0.↵The adaptive Bayesian logistic regression model was used to guide PAN dose escalation with overdose control at all dose levels.↵The minimum exposure criteria for determining MTD was 6 scheduled doses of PAN and 7 scheduled doses of 5-aza during cycle 1.↵Eleven patients, median 69.0 (60-80), were enrolled to include 9 MDS, 1 AML, and 1 CMML.↵Patients were evaluated at 2 PAN doses; This is an observational consecutive case series of patients identified from a registry.
Data were collected by retrospective chart review of patients treated by our toxicology service with this protocol from February 2007 until March 2010.

<AE>Hypokalemia</AE> (defined as less than 3.0 mEq/L) developed in eight patients.
This case pertains to the patient number 4 of 12.

The patient was admitted due to unexplained epileptic convulsions (events onset date unknown).
After measuring hormone levels it was established that all hormonal axes were disturbed.
The cortisol blood level was increased and no longer responding to ACTH stimulation.
The levels of the sex hormones testosterone and oestradiol were also greatly increased, while luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) levels were decreased.
The levels of prolactin, insulin-like growth factor-1 and growth hormone that he regularly injected were also increased.
Most likely, the disturbances of consciousness and epileptic convulsions were the result of hypoglycaemia following injection of insulin, which was also above normal when the patient was admitted (insulin level 64 mU/L).
The author reported that the other possible cause for disturbances of consciousness was the use of other medicinal products, misused during and after training such as tramadol, ephedrine and tadalafil.
The patient was advised to stop the use of all food supplements and medicinal products.
At a check-up one month later, the patient no longer had disturbances of consciousness or epileptic convulsions, however the hormonal disturbances persisted, which could have been the result of the depot effect of exogenous hormones.
At a check-up six months later, the hormonal findings were normal, and the patient was free of complaints, but also had reduced muscle mass.

Use of a reduced dosage is recommended in patients with liver and severe renal impairment because <sDrug>tramadol</sDrug> is extensively metabolized in the liver and primarily excreted in the urine.
The authors describe a patient's clinical presentation and outcome with prolonged <AE>hypoglycemia</AE> attributable to acute <sDrug>tramadol poisoning</sDrug>.
They state that available data suggest <sDrug>tramadol</sDrug> ameliorates peripheral glucose metabolism through central activation of mu opioid receptors (MOR) and that central glucose metabolism and peripheral glucose metabolism are therefore likely to be interrelated.
They conclude that <AE>hypoglycemia</AE> should be considered as a possible manifestation of <sDrug>tramadol poisoning</sDrug>.
The risk may be increased in patients with a poor hepatic reserve.
